uncited: Surface Splatting and Lighting is a family of rendering techniques that convert unstructured point clouds into continuous, shaded surfaces by projecting points as splats into a rendering pipeline [S2, unofficial].

It solves sparse dot cloud aliasing and transparency artifacts by assigning each point sample an extent drawn as a small oriented primitive (a splat) carrying a radially decreasing reconstruction kernel [S2, unofficial].

It differs from its parent [EWA Splatting](1069-ewa-splatting.md) by using screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic linear falloff rather than anisotropic, correctly band-limited EWA footprints, trading accurate filtering for a formulation that requires no per-point normals or radii [S2, unofficial].

The family shares the core mechanism of treating each point sample as a local surface patch that is rasterized as a primitive (typically a point sprite or quadrilateral) to cover the area where the underlying surface is expected to exist.
The rendering pipeline accumulates surface attributes (color, normal, depth) from overlapping splats to reconstruct a continuous signal.
Lighting is applied either during the accumulation pass (if normals are available per-splat) or in a deferred screen-space pass using the accumulated normal buffer.
